ABSTRACT
Inverse design based on high‐performance computing ability is an efficient and intuitive design method. In this paper, we employed the
digitized adjoint method to design a symmetric 3‐dB power splitter based on N‐ary digital pattern with an occupied compact footprint of
only 3.25 µm × 2.6 µm. The digitized adjoint method is applied to inverse design and continuously adjusts and updates the relative
permittivity for a cylindrical material filled with the intermediate material to obtain a quasi‐digital pattern and then transforms it into a
quaternary digital pattern. Based on this approach, a symmetrical structure with etching cylindrical radius of 45, 37, and 30 nm was
obtained, which enables the 3‐dB power splitter to achieve a precise 50:50 split ratio in a wide wavelength range from 1.45 to 1.65 µm.
And the excess loss (EL) was less than 1 dB with an operating bandwidth of 200 nm. This approach holds significant potential for
informing the design of high‐performance, compact power splitters.

Introduction
In recent years, the silicon‐on‐insulator (SOI) platform has
become an ideal platform for realizing photonic integrated
circuits due to its high integration density [1]. Photonic devices
are used to manipulate optical fields in multiple dimensions
through the interaction of light with various objects and have
become an integral component within the field of contemporary
optical research [2, 3]. Optical power splitters are fundamental
photonic devices used to split and combine optical signals [4, 5].
To achieve this function, various structures such as Y‐branching
[6], directional coupler (DC) [7], and multimode interference
(MMI) [8] have been proposed. In 2018, by cascading two MMI
couplers of different sizes, Tian et al. [9] proposed a 1 × 3 MMI
coupler with a size of 15 µm × 15 µm and a large working
bandwidth of more than 50 nm. In 2021, Zhang et al. [10]
designed a DC‐based 3‐dB power splitter with a working
bandwidth of more than 50 nm (from 1.54 to 1.59 µm). How-
ever, the design of a traditional power splitter is performed
through a forward design method, which is founded upon es-
tablished physical principles, followed by the estimation of
geometric

and

through experiments or electromagnetic simulations [11–14],
and the dimensions of the designed components are consider-
able, which restricts the high‐density integration of silicon‐
based photonic devices. Therefore, photonic devices based on
inverse design provide an effective method for simultaneously
designing ultra‐compact and highly functional devices [15]. In
2018, Chang et al. [16] proposed a 1 × 2 power splitter by using
an inverse design algorithm, achieving a compact size of
2.88 µm × 2.88 µm. The device performance with an excess loss
(EL) of 1.5 dB, and the corresponding working bandwidth is

approximately 40 nm. In 2020, Xie et al. [17] used an inverse
design algorithm to design a 3‐dB power splitter for three modes
(TE₀, TE₁, and TE₂). The device achieved a compact footprint of
4 µm × 4.5 µm and insertion losses below 1.5 dB over a 40‐nm
working bandwidth. In 2023, Liu et al. [18] used the inverse
design algorithm to design a power splitter with a size of
11.6 µm. The experimental results show that in the wavelength
range of 1.27–1.33 µm, the loss is less than 0.04 dB. Chen et al.
[19] optimized a 2 × 2 3‐dB power splitter with a size of
4.8 µm × 4.8 µm using an inverse design algorithm; the EL at
1550 nm is about 1.15 dB. In 2024, Yang et al. [20] designed a
dual‐mode 3‐dB power splitter; the device features a size of
10 µm × 3.4 µm. Experimental results show that the insertion
loss is 0.7 dB for the TE0 mode at the wavelength of 1550 nm.
Inverse design first determines the function of the final target device
and then uses intelligent algorithms to inversely solve the device
structure [21]. In general, inverse design algorithms can be classified
into digital and analog methods according to the structure type of
silicon‐based devices. The optimization of digital structures has
effectively employed various digital methods, including particle
swarm optimization (PSO) [22], direct binary search (DBS) [23], and
genetic algorithm (GA) [24]. These methods make the structure
restrict the etching shape to obtain the regular shape, which has
enhanced the manufacturability of devices and substantially
reduced the requirements for manufacturing processes. However, as
the functional complexity increases or the number of pattern
pixels grows, the implementation of these optimization methods
becomes an increasingly formidable challenge. On the contrary,
analog algorithms such as topology optimization [25], goal
priority [26], and level set algorithms [27] can enhance more
freedom in structural design. The gradient‐based adjoint
method efficiently acquires the gradient information for all
permittivities within the optimized region through only two
electromagnetic field simulations (forward and adjoint), yet the
irregular device geometry complicates the fabrication process
and poses a risk of converging prematurely to a locally optimal
solution. In 2020, Wang et al. [28] introduced a method of
digital photonic devices based on the principles of adjoint sen-
sitivity analysis and designed a dual‐mode demultiplexer, the
average insertion loss of the mode was 0.68 dB. In 2022, Xu
et al. [29] used the analog and digital topology optimization
(ADTO) method to design a 3‐dB dual‐mode power splitter with
445 nm bandwidth and additional loss of less than 0.83 dB.
These results demonstrated the possibility and reliability of
combining digital and analog algorithms for the efficient design
of
high‐function
and
high‐performance
on‐chip
photonic
devices.
In this work, a symmetric 3‐dB power splitter with an N‐ary digital
pattern is proposed and optimized by the digitized adjoint method,
achieving an exact 50:50 split ratio (SR). The design of the 3‐dB
power splitter demonstrated a compact size of 3.25 µm × 2.6 µm,
and each cell element comprises a silicon cuboid structure with a
central cylinder that can be filled with either air or silicon. Within
the inverse region, we utilized the adjoint method to continuously
and individually adjust the relative permittivity. To enhance the
adjustment process, we incorporated forced biasing to update the
relative permittivity and obtain a quasi‐digital pattern. The digitized
adjoint method was then employed to convert this quasi‐digital
pattern into a quaternary pattern (N = 4), in which the cylinders
with different relative permittivities were replaced by silicon cylin-
ders and air cylinders with 30, 37, and 45 nm. The EL of the device
is less than 1 dB in the wavelength range of 1.45–1.65 µm, and at
1.55 µm, the EL of the device is about 0.4 dB.

Structure Design
The schematic of the 3‐dB power splitter is shown in Figure 1,
and the device is designed on a standard SOI platform with a
2‐µm buried oxide and a 220‐nm top silicon layer. Specifically,
the 3‐dB power splitter has a footprint of 3.25 µm × 2.6 µm and
is discretized into 20 × 25 pixels for inverse design, each pixel is
a rectangular element with dimensions of 130 nm × 130 nm ×
220 nm. The width of the input is chosen to be 900 nm, output1
and output2 waveguides are 500 nm, and the gap distance
between the two output waveguides is set to be 1 µm to decrease
energy coupling. In the initial structure, the center of each pixel
contains a cylinder with a radius of 45 nm and a depth of
220 nm.
To simplify the calculation, the inverse design figure‐of‐merit
(FOM) for the power splitter is defined as the fundamental
transverse electric mode (TE0) transmitted in the output1 and
output2 waveguides. Since the 3‐dB power splitter is symmetric,
the transmission efficiency of the two output ports is the same,
so that the FOM can be expressed as twice the transmission
efficiency of the TE0 mode in the output1 waveguide, we define
the FOM as follows:

In the last stage, the quasi‐digital pattern of cylindrical material
between air and silicon is transformed into a structure with only
silicon and air. We use a binary pattern (N = 2) to demonstrate,
and the relative permittivity range is divided into two segments
with an intermediate point of 6.5. Cylinders with relative per-
mittivity larger than 6.5 will be replaced with silicon patterns,
whereas those below 6.5 will be replaced by air patterns.
Obviously, it can be evident from Figure 4c that this simple
division greatly increases the device loss, so we introduced a
more comprehensive division of the relative permittivity. The
basic operation is to replace the 45‐nm cylinder with an inter-
mediate dielectric constant in the quasi‐digital pattern with a
45‐nm silicon cylinder, a 45‐nm air cylinder, or an air cylinder
smaller than 45 nm. After 50 iterations, the evolution trend of
FOM and EL is shown in Figure 2b.

Results and Discussion
The digitized adjoint method offers a robust approach that en-
hances the quasi‐digital pattern obtained in the initial stage
through multivalued processing. This innovative method tran-
scends traditional binary processing by providing versatile
options, including ternary processing and more refined quan-
titative grading. The quasi‐digital structure obtained in the first
stage is multivalued to obtain a ternary (N = 3) digital structure
device. The range of the relative permittivity from 1 to 12 is
divided into three segments, with 3.75 and 9.25 as intermediate
points. To achieve optimal performance and ensure precision in
the design, cylinders with relative permittivity larger than 9.25
or less than 3.75 will be replaced with silicon or air patterns,
respectively. Conversely, cylinders within the 3.75–9.25 range
will be substituted with smaller air cylinders, all etched to a
depth of 220 nm. The initial radius of the smaller air cylinders
starts at 30 nm and will be incrementally increased by 1 nm up
to 44 nm. After 15 rounds of simulation, the group exhibiting
the best performance will determine the final radius for these
smaller air cylinders. After simulation polling, the radius of the
smaller air cylinder is taken to be 30 nm. The cylinders filled
with relative permittivity material were eventually replaced
with air cylinders of 45 nm radius, 30 nm air cylinders, and
silicon in the final ternary device structure. As illustrated in
Figure 4d, the device performance for five groups highlights the
effective variation in the radius of the smaller air cylinders from
30 to 44 nm.
The SR of the two output ports is maintained at 1 in the wa-
velength 1.45–1.65 µm, as shown in Figure 4b, the symmetric
structure achieves a perfect SR of 50:50. Here, we define the EL

Comparing binary and ternary processing, the ternary approach
demonstrates superior performance, substantiating that employing
multilevel quantization effectively reduces quantization error and
enhances the device's performance. To enhance the accuracy of the
quantization of the relative permittivity, we advance our initial
ternary pattern by implementing a more granular division, thereby
proving additional digital structure patterns.
The range of the relative permittivity from 1 to 12 is divided into
four segments, with 2.75, 6.5, and 10.25 as intermediate points.
Within the framework of the ternary structure, we established
that the radii of the two air cylinders are 45 and 30 nm, respec-
tively. The radius of the third cylinder gradually decreases from 44
to 31 nm, and the group with the best performance is selected.
And according to the simulation results, we determine the
radius of 37 nm. Cylinders with relative permittivity larger than
10.25 or less than 2.75 will be replaced with silicon or air
pattern, respectively. Conversely, cylinders' relative permittivity
within the 2.75–6.5 range will be substituted with 37‐nm air

The quaternary structure power splitter is shown in Figure 5a,
and the etching depth of all cylinders is 220 nm.
The quaternary (N = 4) structure pattern device obtained
through the optimization process is simulated over a wide
spectrum and compared with the quasi‐digital, binary, and
ternary patterns. Figure 5c shows the EL, whereas Figure 5b
shows the SR of the device; simulation results reveal that the
power splitter could evenly split the input light over an opera-
tion bandwidth of 200 nm. The 1‐dB bandwidth still exceeds
200 nm (from 1.45 to 1.65 µm), and at 1.55 µm, the EL is
about 0.4 dB.
This indicates that ternary quantization introduces greater
quantization errors than quaternary quantization, which dem-
onstrates superior performance. Additionally, the steady‐state
electric field intensity distribution of the quaternary digital
structure pattern device has been simulated, as shown in the
illustration in Figure 5b.

Conclusion
In summary, the digitized adjoint method has been employed in
the design of a symmetric 3‐dB power splitter. This approach
benefits from the advantages of both digital and adjoint
methods, and the device size is 3.25 μm × 2.6 μm. Compared
with the conventional etching of the air cylinder with a
radius of 45 nm, we etched the air cylinders with a radius of
45, 37, and 30 nm; the device performance has been im-
proved. The optical power splitter exhibits an effective 3‐dB
power beam splitting effect by the symmetrical structure.
Meanwhile, the EL for the device is below 1 dB, in the wa-
velength range from 1.45 to 1.65 μm. The 3‐dB power splitter
designed by the combination of adjoint and digital methods
shows great potential for application in the field of high‐
density silicon‐based photonic integration, with the capacity
for extension to the design of numerous additional on‐chip
optical devices.

Abstract: Inverse design based on high‐performance computing ability is an efficient and intuitive design method. In this paper, we employed the digitized adjoint method to design a symmetric 3‐dB power splitter based on N‐ary digital pattern with an occupied compact footprint of only 3.25 µm × 2.6 µm. The digitized adjoint method is applied to inverse design and continuously adjusts and updates the relative permittivity for a cylindrical material filled with the intermediate material to obtain a quasi‐digital pattern and then transforms it into a quaternary digital pattern. Based on this approach, a symmetrical structure with etching cylindrical radius of 45, 37, and 30 nm was obtained, which enables the 3‐dB power splitter to achieve a precise 50:50 split ratio in a wide wavelength range from 1.45 to 1.65 µm. And the excess loss (EL) was less than 1 dB with an operating bandwidth of 200 nm. This approach holds significant potential for informing the design of high‐performance, compact power splitters.
